passage:
Warden's note, Block C, Room 14. Rukmini Iyer, 7 March.
Heard raised voices at 10 pm and went up. Sujay, pointing at the bins, had said that Kamal "never does anything around here." Kamal did not answer about the bins. Instead he listed, fast and loud: he had paid for the gas cylinder, fixed the fan, cleaned the bathroom twice last week, carried Sujay's parcel up four floors. His hands were shaking. Every item was a defence, as if he were on trial. The bins were still full when I arrived. I asked both to sit. I said to Kamal, "It sounds like you felt called lazy." He nodded, jaw tight. To Sujay: "What do you need, specifically?" "Just the bins on Tuesdays." Plan: rota on the door by tomorrow. Will check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Kamal say he had fixed?
qa.a: He said he had fixed the fan.

qa.q: Why did Kamal answer with a list instead of talking about the bins?
qa.a: He felt hurt at being called lazy, so, hands shaking, he defended himself with everything he had done instead of talking about the bins.

qa.q: How did Rukmini Iyer turn the trial back into a request?
qa.a: Rukmini named Kamal's hurt, "you felt called lazy", and asked Sujay for a specific need, which turned out to be only the bins on Tuesdays.

qa.q: What was it like for Sujay to hear a long list in reply?
qa.a: Sujay probably felt unheard, since the bins were never addressed and the complaint became a contest over who does more.

grounding: Shows a flatmate hearing a complaint as an attack on his character and answering with a defensive list, turning a request into a trial.

passage:
12 November, late.
Parul said it tonight, standing in the kitchen doorway: "Do you ever notice anything in this flat?" And I just went off. Not shouting exactly, but listing. I paid the internet bill. I called the plumber. I bought the rice last week, and the detergent. I took out the recycling on Sunday. I heard myself going on and on, like a lawyer. She had only asked about the milk going sour in the fridge. I didn't even answer that. I was too busy proving I'm not a useless flatmate. Maybe it's Mummy's old line, "my son never lifts a finger," still stuck in my head. Now it's 1 am and I feel stupid and also still annoyed. Why did one question feel like she was calling me a bad person?
— Harish

qa.q: What had Parul actually asked about?
qa.a: She had only asked about the milk going sour in the fridge.

qa.q: Why did one question feel so big to Harish?
qa.a: He heard it as being called a useless, bad flatmate, perhaps echoing Mummy's old line, so he rushed to defend himself.

qa.q: What could Harish do tomorrow to get back to the real request?
qa.a: He could tell Parul he got defensive, then ask what she needs about the fridge and the milk and agree on it.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt watching Harish list everything he'd done?
qa.a: Parul may have felt confused and shut out, since a small question about sour milk turned into a trial she never meant to start.

grounding: Shows a young man answering a flatmate's small question with a defensive list, protecting his self-image instead of hearing the request.

passage:
Warden's note, Block C, boys' hostel

At ten tonight I heard raised voices from room 214. Manoj had told Jomon, "You never clean anything, you're so selfish." I stood at the door.
Jomon didn't answer about the room. He started a list: "I paid the electricity share early. I fixed the fan. I bought the mop you use. I cleaned the bathroom Sunday." His voice got faster with each item.
Manoj said, "That's not what I'm talking about." Jomon said, "Then what, I'm on trial now?"
I stepped in and asked them both to sit. I told them I'd help them tomorrow to write down just one thing each wants changed.

qa.q: What did Jomon say he fixed?
qa.a: He said he fixed the fan.

qa.q: Why did Jomon answer with a list of everything he had done?
qa.a: He felt accused of being selfish and defensive about his character, so he tried to prove himself rather than hear the request.

qa.q: What turning point did the warden offer?
qa.a: The warden stepped in and offered to help each write down one thing they want changed, turning the trial back into a request.

qa.q: What might Manoj be experiencing when Jomon starts listing?
qa.a: He likely feels frustrated and unheard, because his complaint about the room turns into Jomon defending his whole character.

grounding: A warden records a young man hearing a complaint as an attack on his character and answering with a list of what he has done.

passage:
Tuesday night

Noor left a sticky note on my door: "Some of us actually buy groceries." That's it. No hello.
I read it and my face went hot. Ma called while I was still standing there, "Suraj beta, all okay?" and I said yes too fast.
Then I went to Noor's room and started listing. I bought the rice last week. I paid the gas guy. I took out the bins twice when it was her turn. I got louder with each thing. She just said, "Okay, you're amazing, I get it," and shut the door.
Now I'm lying here thinking I didn't hear what she actually wanted. I was too busy proving I'm not a freeloader.

qa.q: What did Noor's sticky note say?
qa.a: "Some of us actually buy groceries."

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he read the note?
qa.a: He felt stung and defensive, as if his character was under attack, so his face went hot and he rushed to prove himself.

qa.q: What turning point does Suraj notice he missed?
qa.a: Instead of listing what he had done, he could have asked Noor what she needed, like a grocery plan, so the note became a request, not a trial.

qa.q: What might Noor be experiencing when she shuts the door?
qa.a: She seems frustrated and unheard, feeling that her request turned into an argument about who is better.

grounding: A young man hears a flatmate's complaint as an attack on his character and defends himself with a list, turning a request into a trial.

passage:
Farida: Eshaan bhai, the bins have been full since Friday. The whole kitchen smells.
Eshaan: are you serious? I did the bins last week. and the week before
Eshaan: I also cleaned the fridge, paid the wifi, and bought the dish soap that you use every day
Farida: I'm not saying you never do anything
Eshaan: sounds like it
Eshaan: maybe list what YOU did this month
Farida: I just wanted the bins done tonight 😕
Eshaan stared at his last message. His thumbs were still ready with more. Somewhere in there, a small request about bins had become a court case about whether he was lazy.

qa.q: How long had the bins been full, according to Farida?
qa.a: Since Friday.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan reply with a list of everything he had done?
qa.a: He felt accused of being lazy and got defensive, protecting his image instead of hearing a simple request.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Eshaan now?
qa.a: He could say "Okay, I'll do them tonight," and talk about sharing chores later, instead of adding more to the list.

qa.q: What is Farida experiencing as Eshaan's list grows?
qa.a: She feels hurt and frustrated, because she only wanted the bins done and now feels like she is on trial too.

grounding: A young man hears a flatmate's bin request as an attack on his character and replies with a list, turning a request into a trial.

passage:
The two rooms above the grocery shop in Sirsa were cheap, and Vijay and Amandeep had shared them since the start of their ITI course.

Amandeep came back from the tap with a scowl. "The water drum's empty again, Vijay. You never fill it."

Vijay felt the words land like an accusation in court. "Never? I filled it Monday. And Wednesday. Who swept the stairs on Sunday? Who paid the milkman when you forgot? Who fixed the fan?"

"I'm just saying the drum—"

"You're saying I'm lazy." Vijay's voice climbed. "I cook four nights out of seven. You want a list? I'll write you a list."

Amandeep went quiet. He had only wanted someone to fill the drum. Now he was somehow on trial, and so was Vijay, and neither of them had touched the drum.

qa.q: Where were the two rooms?
qa.a: They were above the grocery shop in Sirsa.

qa.q: Why did Vijay reply with a list of everything he had done?
qa.a: He heard Amandeep's complaint as an attack on his character and felt defensive, needing to prove he wasn't lazy.

qa.q: What could Vijay try next time a complaint feels like an attack?
qa.a: He could first ask what Amandeep actually needs, like a turn system for the drum, before defending himself.

qa.q: How is Amandeep affected by Vijay's reply?
qa.a: Amandeep is taken aback, having only wanted the drum filled, and now feels caught in an argument about who is the better flatmate.

grounding: A flatmate hears a complaint as an attack on his character and answers with a list of his contributions, turning a request into a trial.
